{{DISPLAYTITLE:''K''-groups of a field}}
In mathematics, especially in [[algebraic K-theory|algebraic ''K''-theory]], the '''algebraic ''K''-group of a field''' is important to compute. For a finite field, the complete calculation was given by [[Daniel Quillen]].

==Low degrees==
The map sending a finite-dimensional ''F''-vector space to its dimension induces an isomorphism
:<math>K_0(F) \cong \mathbf Z</math>
for any field ''F''. Next, 
:<math>K_1(F) = F^\times,</math> 
the [[multiplicative group]] of ''F''.<ref>{{harvnb|Weibel|2013|loc=Ch. III, Example 1.1.2.}}</ref>
The second K-group of a field is described in terms of generators and relations by [[Matsumoto's theorem (K-theory)|Matsumoto's theorem]].

== Finite fields ==
The K-groups of finite fields are one of the few cases where the K-theory is known completely:<ref>{{harvnb|Weibel|2013|loc=Ch. IV, Corollary 1.13.}}</ref> for <math>n \ge 1</math>,
:<math>K_n(\mathbb{F}_q) = \pi_n(BGL(\mathbb{F}_q)^+) \simeq 
\begin{cases}
\mathbb{Z}/{(q^i - 1)}, & \text{if }n = 2i - 1 \\
0, & \text{if }n\text{ is even}
\end{cases}</math>
For ''n''=2, this can be seen from Matsumoto's theorem, in higher degrees it was computed by Quillen in conjunction with his work on the [[Adams conjecture]]. A different proof was given by {{harvtxt|Jardine|1993}}.

== Local and global fields ==
{{harvtxt|Weibel|2005}} surveys the computations of K-theory of [[global field]]s (such as [[number field]]s and [[Algebraic function field|function field]]s), as well as [[local field]]s (such as [[p-adic number]]s).

== Algebraically closed fields==
{{harvtxt|Suslin|1983}} showed that the torsion in K-theory is insensitive to extensions of algebraically closed fields. This statement is known as [[Suslin rigidity]].
